references.text: Elijah raises the widow's son in Zarephath from the dead. The parallel is clear: a widow who loses her only son, and a prophet who brings him back to life. Jesus repeats and surpasses Elijah's act.
Elisha raises the Shunammite's son from the dead. Here too, it concerns a mother's only son who dies and is brought back to life by a man of God.

Jairus' daughter is described as his only daughter (μονογενής), the same word used for the widow's son in Nain. Luke emphasizes that it involves an only child in both cases, which underscores the tragedy.
The man cries out to Jesus for help for his son and says he is his only one (μονογενής). Luke again uses this word to emphasize the deep sorrow of losing one's only child.
The immediate continuation shows Jesus' reaction: He feels compassion, commands the dead to rise, and gives him back to his mother—a clear parallel to Elijah in 1 Kings 17:23.
Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead. Here too there is grief and many mourners present, and Jesus intervenes with divine power over death.
Peter raises Tabitha from the dead. The widows weeping around her remind us of the crowd that followed the widow in Nain. The pattern of mourning and resurrection is repeated.
Isaac is referred to as Abraham's only son (יְחִידְךָ), pointing to the deep loss of losing a beloved son. Luke's use of μονογενής (only) gives similar emotional weight.
Zechariah prophesies about grief over 'the only one' (יָחִיד), a deep sorrow like that for a firstborn son. The motif of mourning an only son connects this with the widow in Nain's grief.
Jeremiah uses the image of grief over an only son (יָחִיד) as an expression of deepest sorrow. The widow in Nain who loses her only son represents exactly this kind of grief.
